Document 2: As the sun dipped below the Oklahoma horizon, casting a warm orange glow over the University of Tulsa's campus, Charles Archambo laced up his sneakers for the final time. As he walked off the court, sweat-drenched and defeated, Charles couldn't shake the feeling that there was more to life than the hardwood. That summer, Charles made a bold decision: he would trade in his sneakers for skates. He packed his bags and headed to Toronto, where he'd heard rumors of a fledgling hockey league looking for talent. The National Hockey League, they called it. Charles arrived in Toronto with a suitcase full of dreams and a heart full of determination. He spent long hours on the ice, honing his skills and learning the intricacies of the game. It wasn't easy – the Canadians were a tough bunch, and they didn't take kindly to some college basketball player thinking he could just waltz in and join their ranks. But Charles was no stranger to hard work. He'd spent countless hours in the gym, perfecting his jump shot and building his endurance. And it paid off. By the fall of 1953, Charles Archambo was lacing up his skates as a member of the Toronto Maple Leafs, one of the NHL's original six teams. As he took to the ice for his first game, the crowd's murmurs of curiosity turned to cheers of excitement. This kid from Tulsa, Oklahoma, was a natural. He skated with a fluid grace, his stickhandling skills honed from years of dribbling a basketball. The NHL had never seen anything like him before. And Charles, for his part, had never felt more alive. The rush of adrenaline as he crashed into the boards, the thrill of scoring his first goal – it was all so new, so exhilarating. He knew he'd made the right decision, leaving the basketball court behind for the frozen expanse of the hockey rink. As the final buzzer sounded, Charles grinned from ear to ear, his teeth chattering with excitement.

Use only what the documents say: nothing you know from elsewhere, and no explanation of your own. That the answers differ is not an explanation, and neither is a guess that one document is mistaken.
